title: Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible
lead: Passages written in conflicts between Jews in the first century were later read by Christians as condemnations of the Jewish people as a whole, and fed centuries of contempt and violence. This page gathers those passages, their first meaning, their history of use, and the churches' later repentance.

sections.b: The texts most often used against Jews include "His blood on us, and on our children" (Matthew 27:25), Jesus' woes on scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23), "you are of your father the devil" in John 8:44, the many uses of "the Jews" in John, "the synagogue of Satan" (Revelation 2:9; 3:9), and Paul's words about Jews "who killed the Lord Jesus" (1 Thessalonians 2:14–16). Each was written within a quarrel among Jews or between Jesus' followers and the synagogues of their towns. Most of the writers were Jews themselves.
sections.refs: Matthew 23:1–36; Matthew 27:25; John 8:44; 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16; Revelation 2:9; Revelation 3:9

sections.b: From the second century on, Christian writers such as Melito of Sardis and John Chrysostom turned these texts into a charge of deicide against all Jews. The charge shaped laws, sermons and passion plays, and was used to justify expulsions and massacres, and later Nazi propaganda. After the Holocaust, Jules Isaac named this "the teaching of contempt." The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected collective guilt; Protestant churches, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994), repudiated Luther's anti-Jewish writings; and Jewish scholars answered with Dabru Emet (2000). Reading these passages faithfully today means keeping their words and knowing their history.
